messages.subject: point prediction in INLA
messages.subject_clean: point prediction in INLA
messages.body_plain:
Hi
I want to predict the number of an event for some points by considering the effect of environmental covariates over time. I used spatio-temporal model and the model is like below:

       result <- inla(y ~ -1+ resi.mean + rec.mean + comer.mean + trans.mean + f(index,model=spde,group= index.group,  control.group= list(model='ar1')),
              family = 'nbinomial', data=inla.stack.data(stack), control.predictor=list(A=inla.stack.A(stack), compute= TRUE, link=1))

The question is why result$summary.fitted.values is NULL even though control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE , link =1)?

I'm really thankful for your help.

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Bias in spatial covariance estimates in simulations
messages.body_plain:
Hi Haakon and Finn,

Thanks very much to both of you for the response. I took some time to change up some of my code to address the comments you made.

To address Haakon's comments, my width was originally [0,15]x[0,15] (so width is 15), but I scale the coordinates down to [0,1]x[0,1] so that the scaled width is 1.
As such, the true range was sqrt(8)/1 = 2.8, but when I scale the coordinates, this becomes sqrt(8)/15 = 0.189.
I have tried numerous settings for different mesh arguments; my max.edge length that showed the best results (in terms of covering true theta1 and theta2 in the 95% credible interval) was max.edge = c(.1,.3) (see below)
My outer mesh extension was 2.8 but I switched that to be 0.2 after scaling the coordinates.

Finn, I rewrote some of my code to evaluate performance in terms of theta1 and theta2, as well as checked to see how often the truth was contained in the credible intervals for the nugget, sigma2, kappa, emp_range, theta1 and theta2. The results for my best mesh settings and number of sims are shown below, as well as the proportion of the 301 sims that covered the truth in the credible interval.

in_edges out_edges prec1 prec2  cutoff  offset   sims                      sig2cover  tau2cover   kappacover   rangecover   theta1cover  theta2cover
          0.1            0.3 1e-04 1e-04  0.035      0.1    301                    0.8571429                0    0.9202658    0.9202658      0.9269103   0.9202658

Of course, each of these would ideally be close to 95%. Sigma2 starts to drop down a bit below the others near 86%, while the nugget (so the inverse of the precision) is always estimated much too high (around 0.05 instead of 0.01). I would think that an overestimate of the nugget would mean an underestimate for sigma2; however, both of these are typically overestimated. (Please see the attached pdf for the results of some of the posterior means and medians of different parameters; the maroon line is the true value). Do you know why both of these are overestimated? Considering my simulations have over 10,000 data points each, I expected these estimates to be a little closer to the truth. Please let me know any other comments you have regarding these results or my code (also attached). Thanks again for your helpful input!

Steve

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Bias in spatial covariance estimates in simulations
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

You haven’t mentioned how you’ve set all your prior distributions. These can/should have an impact on the results. Also be aware that even under exact observations and exact calculations under infill asymptotics, kappa, and therefore also the range, isn’t consistently estimable, so you should not expect perfect coverage even at the best of times for that parameter. The correct check for Bayesian inference methods is to check how close the results are to the true posterior distribution. You can ask for no more from the methods; improvement beyond that will require improvements to the model itself, including the prior distributions.

For a brief intro and a reference to how to do a simulation study for how well inla recovers the true posterior, see for example part 2 in my lecture notes from a summer school earlier this year:

https://www.maths.ed.ac.uk/~flindgre/cuso2019/

Finn

messages.body_plain:
The priors for theta1 and theta2 are highly content dependent. See e.g. the JSS paper with preprint version here http://www.r-inla.org/examples/tutorials/spde-tutorial-from-jss  for one way of reasoning towards potentially sensible priors. However, nowadays we tend to use penalized complexity priors instead of lognormal priors for the SPDE parameters. See the help text for inla.spde2.pcmatern for more details.

Finn

> On 2 Dec 2019, at 13:14, Stephen Walsh <wals...@vt.edu> wrote:
>
> ﻿

> Hi, apologies, I forgot to mention the priors specs. I originally used the default N(0,1) on both theta1 and theta2, but I have since been using N(0,.0001) for theta1 and theta2, where .0001 is the precision to see if a more vague prior would give better results. Thanks for sending the resources, I will take a look at those; I appreciate your input.
>
> On Monday, December 2, 2019 at 3:26:17 AM UTC-5, Finn Lindgren wrote:
> > Hi,
> >
> > You haven’t mentioned how you’ve set all your prior distributions. These can/should have an impact on the results. Also be aware that even under exact observations and exact calculations under infill asymptotics, kappa, and therefore also the range, isn’t consistently estimable, so you should not expect perfect coverage even at the best of times for that parameter. The correct check for Bayesian inference methods is to check how close the results are to the true posterior distribution. You can ask for no more from the methods; improvement beyond that will require improvements to the model itself, including the prior distributions.
> >
> > For a brief intro and a reference to how to do a simulation study for how well inla recovers the true posterior, see for example part 2 in my lecture notes from a summer school earlier this year:
> >
> > https://www.maths.ed.ac.uk/~flindgre/cuso2019/
> >
> > Finn
> >
> > > On 1 Dec 2019, at 22:40, Stephen Walsh <wals...@vt.edu> wrote:
> > >
> > > ﻿
> > > Hi Haakon and Finn,
> > >
> > > Thanks very much to both of you for the response. I took some time to change up some of my code to address the comments you made.
> > >
> > > To address Haakon's comments, my width was originally [0,15]x[0,15] (so width is 15), but I scale the coordinates down to [0,1]x[0,1] so that the scaled width is 1.
> > > As such, the true range was sqrt(8)/1 = 2.8, but when I scale the coordinates, this becomes sqrt(8)/15 = 0.189.
> > > I have tried numerous settings for different mesh arguments; my max.edge length that showed the best results (in terms of covering true theta1 and theta2 in the 95% credible interval) was max.edge = c(.1,.3) (see below)
> > > My outer mesh extension was 2.8 but I switched that to be 0.2 after scaling the coordinates.
> > >
> > > Finn, I rewrote some of my code to evaluate performance in terms of theta1 and theta2, as well as checked to see how often the truth was contained in the credible intervals for the nugget, sigma2, kappa, emp_range, theta1 and theta2. The results for my best mesh settings and number of sims are shown below, as well as the proportion of the 301 sims that covered the truth in the credible interval.
> > >
> > > in_edges out_edges prec1 prec2  cutoff  offset   sims                      sig2cover  tau2cover   kappacover   rangecover   theta1cover  theta2cover
> > >           0.1            0.3 1e-04 1e-04  0.035      0.1    301                    0.8571429                0    0.9202658    0.9202658      0.9269103   0.9202658
> > >
> > > Of course, each of these would ideally be close to 95%. Sigma2 starts to drop down a bit below the others near 86%, while the nugget (so the inverse of the precision) is always estimated much too high (around 0.05 instead of 0.01). I would think that an overestimate of the nugget would mean an underestimate for sigma2; however, both of these are typically overestimated. (Please see the attached pdf for the results of some of the posterior means and medians of different parameters; the maroon line is the true value). Do you know why both of these are overestimated? Considering my simulations have over 10,000 data points each, I expected these estimates to be a little closer to the truth. Please let me know any other comments you have regarding these results or my code (also attached). Thanks again for your helpful input!
> > >
> > > Steve
> > >
> > > On Monday, November 18, 2019 at 3:18:56 AM UTC-5, Finn Lindgren wrote:
> > > > ...and also, check the credible intervals rather than just the posterior mean, to see if the bias is small compared with the uncertainty ty. Also, the posterior mean should not be expected to be an unbiased estimator, so you need to consider your priors as well. The posterior mean is also dependent on the transformation scale. The posteriors for precision parameters tend to be more symmetric on the log scale, so you should do the comparison on that scale as well.
> > > > Finally, take a look at the author’s discussion response in the 2011 Lindgren et al paper, where we discussed biases due to coarse mesh resolution.
> > > >
> > > > Finn
> > > >
> > > > > On 18 Nov 2019, at 09:03, Haakon Bakka <ba...@r-inla.org> wrote:
> > > > >
> > > > > ﻿
> > > > > Can you compute, and double-check that you have the right
> > > > > - Width of the domain (15?)
> > > > > - Empirical range (truth) (2.8?)
> > > > > - Max.edge.length (I guess you used 0.2 or less?)
> > > > > - Outer mesh extension (2.8 width?)
> > > > >
> > > > > Attach the plot of a simulation, and plot(mesh).
> > > > >
> > > > > Best,
> > > > > Haakon
> > > > >
> > > > >
> > > > > On Mon, 18 Nov 2019 at 02:44, Stephen Walsh <wals...@vt.edu> wrote:
> > > > > > Hi there,
> > > > > >
> > > > > > I am simulating data with zero mean and Matern spatial covariance parameters such that:
> > > > > >
> > > > > > alpha = 2 (so nu = 1)
> > > > > > nugget effect (sigma^2_epsilon) = .01
> > > > > > marginal variance (sigma^2_omega) = .5
> > > > > > spatial range parameter kappa = 1
> > > > > >
> > > > > > I am using functions inla.mesh.2d, inla.spde2.matern, inla.spde.make.A and inla to estimate these spatial parameters. I have modeled them with multiple different settings: I have tried using different values for the mesh max.edges, cutoff, offset, using the loc vs loc.domain. I have tried different prior precisions for theta1 and theta2 as well. I have also tried centering and/or scaling the spatial coordinates (they were originally on 0 to 15 by 0 to 15 square, with approximately 10000 data points).
> > > > > >
> > > > > > When I look at my results for 150 simulations for each of the multiple different mesh settings and prior settings, my results are typically biased in the following way:
> > > > > >
> > > > > > the average nugget estimate is in the range 0.019-0.05 (truth .01)
> > > > > > the marginal variance is estimated around .6-.7 (truth .5)
> > > > > > the range is usually estimated around .75 (truth 1) [or estimated around 12 when the truth is 15 if I scale the coordinates]
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Do you have any ideas as why these biases exist? I have tried so many combinations that I thought I would have found something that works by now. Thanks for any insight, please let me know if you have questions. Thanks very much for your help and expertise!
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Steve

messages.subject: Huge range for SPDE - changing posterior range does not help
messages.subject_clean: Huge range for SPDE - changing posterior range does not help
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone

I've fitted a Poisson GLM with a random intercept and a PC mattern spatial random effect to predict species richness for the US.

The model fits the data well, however, the posterior range of the spatial field is enormous (5000 km) and I can't find out, what exactly is the cause of it. Moreover, this is a larger value than the range that I've defined for the prior median range: 3200 (I chose 1/2 of the study area's extend as a very large starting point). My initial plan was to run it once with such a large posterior range to get a better Idea of the actual range - now I'm puzzled about the result and have trouble finding the cause of this unreasonable range.

So far I checked to reduce the prior range, gradually going down and approaching a range I would find meaningful, from the initial 3200 to 1000, 500, 400, 300, 200, 100. But the posterior range remained unchanged at around 5000. Furthermore, when lowering the median range to 100 or lower, I received the following error message:

    GMRFLib version 3.0-0-snapshot, has recived error no [12]
    Reason    : The Newton-Raphson optimizer did not converge
    Message   : Condition `lambda < 1.0 / lambda_lim' is not TRUE
    Function  : GMRFLib_init_GMRF_approximation_store__intern
    File      : approx-inference.c
    Line      : 2899

    Variable evaluates to NAN or INF. idx=(9464,9464). I will try to fix it...

    Variable evaluates to NAN or INF. idx=(9464,9464). I will try to fix it...
    file: smtp-taucs.c  hgid: b84cb08f11c9  date: Thu Jul 12 13:38:25 2018 +0300
    Function: GMRFLib_build_sparse_matrix_TAUCS(), Line: 751, Thread: 0
    Variable evaluates to NAN or INF. idx=(9464,9464). I will try to fix it...Error in inla.inlaprogram.has.crashed()

I read other posts on this error message in this mailing list and it often seemed to be a matter of scale, or of choosing more constraining starting values (which I did for the prior median range). As for the scale: The Lat/Long is converted into km and I do get a "result". In other cases with the same issue converting to km did often fixed it.

My environmental covariates represent % coverage of the respective Land cover class around the transects (range 0-1), climatic variables have been centered and scaled, altogether there's 4 time-steps with available data. I'm actually working with a spatio-temporal model, but to reduce complexity, I have rerun the simpler model here and it yields the same error.

Below is some of the code and the summary for the model. Attached is the verbose = TRUE output for the model and an image of the mesh, in case the error may originate from there..

#~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ Making the Mesh #
 # changing the CRS unit from meters to kilometers to avoid numerical precision errors
 Loc.crs.m <- CRS(proj4string(Loc.shp))
 Loc.crs.km <- inla.CRS(Loc.crs.m, args = list(units="km"))

 Loc <- cbind (BBS$LONG_X, BBS$LAT_Y)
 Loc.km <- Loc / 1000 # conversion into km

 RangeGuess <- 500
 MaxEdge <- RangeGuess / 5
 mesh1 <- inla.mesh.2d(Loc.km,
                       max.edge = c(1, 5) * MaxEdge,
                       cutoff = MaxEdge / 5,
                       crs = Loc.crs.km)

 mesh1$n
 # 3938

 #~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ Projecttor Matrix #
 A2      <- inla.spde.make.A (mesh  = mesh1,    #mesh without temporal dependency
                              loc   = Loc.km)

 #~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ Define the SPDE #
 diff (range (mesh1$loc[ , 1]))/2
 #  3243.851
 prior.median.range = 3200

 sd (BBS$Species.Richness_MEAN) / 10
 # 1.442036
 prior.median.sd = 1.5

 spde1 <- inla.spde2.pcmatern (mesh1,
                               prior.range = c (prior.median.range, 0.05),
                               prior.sigma = c (prior.median.sd, 0.05))

 #~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ Define the Spatial Field #
 w.st2    <- inla.spde.make.index (   # only for the spatial effects, without temporal effect
   name   = "w_spat",
   n.spde = spde1$n.spde)

 #~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ Make the Stack #
 X <- data.frame (Year                              = BBS$Year,
                  Year2                                   = BBS$Year2,
                  rteno_factor                            = BBS$rteno_factor,
                  POP_peoplePerKm2                  = BBS$POP_peoplePerKm2,
                  LC_Crop_dominatedLCs              = BBS$LC_Crop_dominatedLCs,
                  LC_Herbaceous_dominatedLCs        = BBS$LC_Herbaceous_dominatedLCs,
                  LC_Needleleaved_dominatedLCs      = BBS$LC_Needleleaved_dominatedLCs,
                  LC_Broadleaved_dominatedLCs  = BBS$LC_Broadleaved_dominatedLCs,
                  LC_Shrub_dominatedLCs            = BBS$LC_Shrub_dominatedLCs,
                  LC_Grasslands                            = BBS$LC_Grasslands,
                  LC_Urban                                     = BBS$LC_Urban,
                  LC_SparseVeg_dominatedLCs    = BBS$LC_SparseVeg_dominatedLCs,
                  LC_Flood_dominatedLCs            = BBS$LC_Flood_dominatedLCs,
                  LC_BareLand_dominatedLCs     = BBS$LC_BareLand_dominatedLCs,
                  LC_Waterbodies                          = BBS$LC_Waterbodies,
                  LC_Ice_permanent                      = BBS$LC_Ice_permanent,
                  BIOCLIM_01_ztrans                    = BBS$BIOCLIM_01_ztrans,
                  BIOCLIM_04_ztrans                    = BBS$BIOCLIM_04_ztrans,
                  BIOCLIM_12_ztrans                    = BBS$BIOCLIM_12_ztrans)

 Stack2 <- inla.stack (
   tag = "Fit",
   data = list (y = BBS$Species.Richness_MEAN),
   A = list (A2, 1),  # the projector matrix
   effects = list (
     w_spat = w.st2, #spatio-temporal field
     X = as.data.frame(X) # covariates
   ))

 #~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ Forumla #
 fSR <-y ~ -1 + LC_Crop_dominatedLCs + LC_Herbaceous_dominatedLCs +
   LC_Needleleaved_dominatedLCs + LC_Broadleaved_dominatedLCs +
   LC_Grasslands + LC_Urban + LC_SparseVeg_dominatedLCs + LC_Flood_dominatedLCs +
   LC_BareLand_dominatedLCs + LC_Waterbodies +
   BIOCLIM_01_ztrans + BIOCLIM_04_ztrans + BIOCLIM_12_ztrans +
   f (rteno_factor, model = "iid") + # random intercept for each transect
   f (w_spat, model = spde1) # spatial term

 #~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ Running the model #
 inla.setOption (scale.model.default = TRUE)

 M.SR <- inla (fSR,
              family = "poisson",
              data = inla.stack.data(Stack2),
              control.compute = list(dic = TRUE, waic = TRUE),
              control.predictor = list (compute = TRUE,
                                        A = inla.stack.A(Stack2)),
              verbose = TRUE)

messages.body_plain:
5000 is quite similar to 3200, so for the run with 3200 as prior median, 5000 sounds perfectly reasonable...

But I wonder about your coordinates. What is the initial coordinate system/CRS? Your “conversion” seems to take raw long&lat values and divide by 1000, but long&lat aren’t in metres, they’re in degrees, so that conversion doesn’t seem to make sense. Also, setting units open a CRS only makes sense if that CRS knows about distance units, e.g. UTM.

Finn

Hello Finn,

thanks for your quick response and my appologies for not making all this a bit clearer in the beginning.

About the range: would you still expect such a high posterior range, when setting the prior.median.range = c (200, 0.05) ? I was a bit surprised that it didn't seem to make any difference for the posterior distribution and then crashed when I tried to use smaller (but what I thought more reasonable ranges). Under which conditions would a range that spans almost across the entire US ba a reasonable thing to expect?

What I've called Lat/Long is infect the Easting/Nothing with the exact same coordinates as in the shapefile, I just loaded the shapefile in order to provide the mesh with a CRS-object - following some earlier struggle with the mesh <http://www.r-inla.org/?place=msg%2Fr-inla-discussion-group%2FPtkFmEHujdk%2FUNg4TZEeEAAJ>. The CRS is Albers equal area with the units being meters. That's why I thought conversion to km would be fine by dividing by 1000, or am I missing something?

messages.body_plain:
Hi, all-

Bayesian disease mapping using INLA seems to be a great alternative to the frequentist approach to Small Area Estimation (SAE)--viz., multi-level modelling. Still, one weakness seems to be that INLA doesn't produce estimates (as far as I know) for areal units that don't have outcome data. Multi-level modelling would produce estimates for a geographical unit on which there is no information (say, a multi-stage sample survey that didn't include residents of a given ZIP Code) by using the parameters of the global, fixed effects--that is, the "synthetic estimate"--to produce an ZIP Code-level estimate of the quantity of interest.  The intuition is that the geographical unit with no information on outcomes is similar to other units that do have information.

What's the analogous Bayesian disease mapping approach?  And, how is it implemented in R-INLA?

Thanks,
David

just a note: range is a scale parameter, so that the 'error' is
relative, so it better to compare the estimate with the truth like the
ratio

	range.est/range.true

rather than

	|range.est - range.true|

which gives less meaning

messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA group,

I am doing an independent project to map vaccine hesitance in Europe, this is a Eurobarometer database with NUTS 2 and NUTS 3 in the database.

I tried to smooth the hesitancy proportions with an INLA model but it is not converging. I was wondering if I could get some help from you.

I think the error could be:
The database is a mixture of NUTS 1 2 and 3 and the shapefile is NUTS2, this could be the source of error. However I dont know how to dissolve boundaries in shapefiles. If you think thats the error could you help me?

Maybe is something else that I am not getting

Thank you

The repo for reproducubility is open on my GitHub,
https://github.com/aperaltasantos/vaccines_eurobarometer/blob/master/vaccine_script.Rmd

The code is also posted
## Set INLA
```{r, echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, tidy = TRUE, tidy.opts = list(width.cutoff=40)}
library(spdep)
EU_NUTS.neigh <- poly2nb(EU_NUTS)
library(INLA)
nb2INLA('EU_NUTS.neigh.graph',EU_NUTS.neigh)
```
## Fit global/local spatial smoothing model
```{r, echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, tidy = TRUE, tidy.opts = list(width.cutoff=40)}
formula = logit.pi ~ 1 +
f(struct, model='besag',
adjust.for.con.comp=TRUE,
constr=TRUE,
graph='EU_NUTS.neigh.graph') +
f(unstruct,model='iid',
param=c(0.5,0.008))
mod.smooth <- inla(formula,
family = "gaussian",
data = data,
control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
control.family = list( hyper = list(prec = list( initial = log(1), fixed=TRUE))),
scale=logit.prec)
# The model does not converge
```

messages.body_plain:
Many thanks!  That seems easy enough.

Quick follow-up:  how are predictions for missing areal units calculated?  I guess the specifics depend on each model, but is there a general form for the predictor or a general principle--e.g., a missing areal unit might be simply the average of all neighbors with non-missing observations?

David

>

>

> On 4 Dec 2019, 04:55 +0300, David Crow <davi...@cide.edu>, wrote:

> > Hi, all-
> >
> > Bayesian disease mapping using INLA seems to be a great alternative to the frequentist approach to Small Area Estimation (SAE)--viz., multi-level modelling. Still, one weakness seems to be that INLA doesn't produce estimates (as far as I know) for areal units that don't have outcome data. Multi-level modelling would produce estimates for a geographical unit on which there is no information (say, a multi-stage sample survey that didn't include residents of a given ZIP Code) by using the parameters of the global, fixed effects--that is, the "synthetic estimate"--to produce an ZIP Code-level estimate of the quantity of interest.  The intuition is that the geographical unit with no information on outcomes is similar to other units that do have information.
> >
> > What's the analogous Bayesian disease mapping approach?  And, how is it implemented in R-INLA?
> >
> > Thanks,
> > David

messages.subject: INLA Crashes with Large Data Sets
messages.subject_clean: INLA Crashes with Large Data Sets
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

As recently reported by others, I am no longer able to use INLA for large data sets. Below is some code for reproducing the problem.

If you run the code, you'll see that a simple model crashes with 100K records but runs with 30K records. I tried a bunch of control.inla and control.compute options, just in case defaults have changed in recent test versions of INLA, but I haven't got it to work. Then I thought I needed to get the Pardiso libraries under the assumption that these were now required for larger data sets. Unfortunately, I am not a computer whiz, and I haven't been able to get Pardiso to work. I downloaded the three Pardiso files for Windows, put them in their own directory (C:/Pardiso) and pointed INLA to the licence, but I get errors (FAILURE: PARDISO IS NOT INSTALLED OR NOT WORKING). I am sure there is more to configuring Pardiso, but have no clue what to do. So, my questions:

(1) Am I doing something wrong in the example code?
(2) If not, can anyone provide detailed configuration for the latest version of Pardiso (6.2) for a Windows machine?
(3) If not, can I somehow download an older version of INLA that still works with large data sets?

Thanks a ton!
Tim

# set up
library(dplyr)
library(INLA)

# make data
n <- 100000
x=ceiling(runif(n, 0, 12))
y=ceiling(100 + 2*x + rnorm(n, x, 10))
dat1 <- data.frame(y, x)
plot(y~x, data=dat1)
head(dat1)
summary(dat1)

# make formula
form1 <- y ~ x

# run model on all data
lm1 <- lm(form1, data=dat1)
inla1 <- inla(form1, data=dat1, verbose=T,
              control.inla=list(strategy="adaptive", int.strategy="eb"),
              control.compute=list(openmp.strategy="default", smtp="default"))
summary(lm1)
summary(inla1)

# thin data
dat2 <- dat1 %>% sample_n(size=30000)

# run model on less data
lm2 <- lm(form1, data=dat2)
inla2 <- inla(form1, data=dat2, verbose=T,
              control.inla=list(strategy="adaptive", int.strategy="eb"),
              control.compute=list(openmp.strategy="default", smtp="default"))
summary(lm2)
summary(inla2)

# need pardiso?
inla.setOption(pardiso.license="C:/Users/tmeehan/pardiso.lic")
inla.pardiso.check()
# inla.pardiso()

messages.body_plain:
I'm new to using INLA, so forgive me if my question is obvious.

I want to model disease incidence spatially using a CAR order 1 model, using a Besag model for spatial autocorrelations along with areal-specific covariates. The problem I have is whether INLA can allow me to use covariates that are themselves estimated.

Specifically, my model assumes that disease incidence in each age group is a function of past incidence (due to built up immunity). Past incidence is unobserved -- indeed, it is the main reason that I am estimating the model. The effect of past incidence on current transmission depends on the age group in question because it depends on the level of transmission they have been exposed to throughout their lives.

So, concretely, suppose that incidence in region, i, in age group, a, at time, t is Poisson distributed,

I_{i, t, a} ~ Poisson(e^lambda_{i, t, a}),

where,

lambda_{i, t, a} = sum_{neighbours_j} nu_j + sum_past_incidence_{tau=1}^{a} e^{-lambda_{i, t - tau, a - tau}}

So the first term on the RHS of the above is the Besag spatial model and the second term is effectively an integral over past transmission.

Can this sort of model be handled in INLA?

Thanks for the swift reply and my apologies for the lack of clarity with my message. Yes, you were right to point out that my model seems a little strange -- think I made a mistake when I wrote it down. I also think that I am missing some of the complexity that I need to include to explain the difficulties I'm having.

Basically, what I want to estimate is a model that looks like (eqns. 1-3 here: https://elifesciences.org/articles/45474 that I repeat below). The fraction of people who have not been exposed to any strain of the disease is:

x_{t, a} = exp(-4\int lambda_{t-tau} dtau)

z1 is the proportion of people who have been exposed to one strain (out of 4):

z1_{t,  a} = exp(-3\int lambda_{t-tau} dtau) (1 - exp(-\int lambda_{t-tau} dtau))

The incidence then is given by the product:

I_{t, a} = 3 lambda_t z1_{t,a}

which is the mean of my Poisson (ignoring any spatial effects).

I'm not sure I can get a useful expression for log (I_{t,a}) because it will involve log (1 - exp(-\int lambda_{t-tau} dtau) - a nonlinear term.

Can this sort of model be estimated in the INLA framework?

messages.body_plain:
Hello Harvard,

what exactly do you mean with range etst./range true?

As for my initial question, which remains unclear: My issue doesn't arise from having the conversion into kilometers, as I'm using Easting/Northing.
I have rerun the models without a CRS in the mesh-creation and for a range of priors, below is the code and results for range 3200 and 100 km, with two different P values for the 100km spde
########### SPDEs
 prior.median.range = 3200 # the initial 3200 km from the first post
 prior.median.sd = 1.5
 spde_3200_km <- inla.spde2.pcmatern (mesh_km,

                                   prior.range = c (prior.median.range, 0.05),
                                   prior.sigma = c (prior.median.sd,    0.05))

 prior.median.range = 100
 spde_100_km            <- inla.spde2.pcmatern (mesh_km,

                                                prior.range = c (prior.median.range, 0.05),
                                                prior.sigma = c (prior.median.sd,    0.05))

 spde_100_otherprior_km <- inla.spde2.pcmatern (mesh_km,
                                                prior.range = c (prior.median.range, 0.5),
                                                prior.sigma = c (prior.median.sd,    0.5))

########### define the spatial field
 w.st_km_1 <- inla.spde.make.index (
   name   = "w_spat",
   n.spde = spde_3200_km$n.spde)
 # same for the two other SPDEs

########### Stacks
 Stack_km_1 <- inla.stack (

   tag = "Fit",
   data = list (y = BBS$Species.Richness_MEAN),

   A = list (A2_km, 1),  # the projector matrix
   effects = list (
     w_spat = w.st_km_1, #spatial field

     X = as.data.frame(X) # covariates
   ))

 # same for the two other stacks

########### Model formulas
 fSR_km_1 <-y ~ -1 + LC_Crop_dominatedLCs + LC_Herbaceous_dominatedLCs +

   LC_Needleleaved_dominatedLCs + LC_Broadleaved_dominatedLCs +
   LC_Grasslands + LC_Urban + LC_SparseVeg_dominatedLCs + LC_Flood_dominatedLCs +
   LC_BareLand_dominatedLCs + LC_Waterbodies +
   BIOCLIM_01_ztrans + BIOCLIM_04_ztrans + BIOCLIM_12_ztrans +
   f (rteno_factor, model = "iid") + # random intercept for each transect

   f (w_spat, model = spde_3200_km) # spatial term
 # same for the two other spde

########### run the models
 inla.setOption (scale.model.default = TRUE)
 M.SR_km_1 <- inla (fSR_km_1,
                   family = "poisson",
                   data = inla.stack.data(Stack_km_1),

                   control.compute = list(dic = TRUE, waic = TRUE),
                   control.predictor = list (compute = TRUE,

                                             A = inla.stack.A(Stack_km_1)),
                   verbose = TRUE)

# same for the two other models

when inspecting the otput I get very similar results:

> M.SR_km_1$summary.hyperpar #range 3200, p 0.05

                                   mean           sd  0.025quant    0.5quant  0.975quant

So, what I gather from that is a) I must have overlooked an error somewhere - any other guesses, where, given that the m to km conversion is correct? Or b) the prior median range and sd have little to no influence on the posterior distribution of the spatial effect and the true range is really this big. To me it is unclear how to interpret a spatial random effect with a range of around ~5000km. Wouldn't this mean that the spatial auto correlation is also extending over almost the entire study area (also see the attached plots)? I just wonder, if this could be the case, and if so, what to make of it?

Last point: if you look at the maps below you can notice that they spatial random field is only positive - that's also something I haven't seen yet and therefore I would like to know if you have suggestions why that is?

Best,
Vincent

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] INLA Now Crashes With Large Data Sets
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] INLA Now Crashes With Large Data Sets
messages.body_plain:
I just set up an Ubuntu VM on my Windows machine, loaded the latest R and R-INLA, and everything works fine. So either I messed up my Windows R configuration somehow, or a Windows update messed it up for me. Anyway, if anyone else has this problem, this is one workaround.

# test

# set up
library(dplyr)
library(INLA)

# make data
n <- 100000
x=ceiling(runif(n, 0, 12))
y=ceiling(100 + 2*x + rnorm(n, x, 10))
dat1 <- data.frame(y, x)
plot(y~x, data=dat1)
head(dat1)
summary(dat1)

# make formula
form1 <- y ~ x

# run model on all data
lm1 <- lm(form1, data=dat1)
inla1 <- inla(form1, data=dat1, verbose=T,
              control.inla=list(strategy="adaptive", int.strategy="eb"),
              control.compute=list(openmp.strategy="default", smtp="default"))
summary(lm1)
summary(inla1)

# thin data
dat2 <- dat1 %>% sample_n(size=30000)

# run model on less data
lm2 <- lm(form1, data=dat2)
inla2 <- inla(form1, data=dat2, verbose=T,
              control.inla=list(strategy="adaptive", int.strategy="eb"),
              control.compute=list(openmp.strategy="default", smtp="default"))
summary(lm2)
summary(inla2)

# need pardiso?
inla.setOption(pardiso.license="C:/Users/tmeehan/pardiso.lic")
inla.pardiso.check()

# inla.pardiso()

messages.body_plain:
range is a scale parameter like stdev, etc, so the error is relative,
(or thevariance of the parameter depends on the parameter), so to
quantify the error, its better to look at the ratio

range.estimated / range.true

and NOT

	| range.estimated - range.true |

shell, like

ulimit $(for opt in c d s t f n; do echo -n "-$opt unlimited ";done)

I would like to obtain 90% rather than 95% credible intervals. I have first testing my approach to see whether I can obtain 95% intervals but they slightly differ from those in the summary output as follows:

inla1$summary.fixed
                    mean          sd   0.025quant     0.5quant   0.975quant         mode          kld

inla.qmarginal(c(0.025,0.975),inla.tmarginal(function(x) x,inla1$marginals.fixed[[2]]))
[1] 6.331829e-05 7.456714e-04

They are almost the same but still a little different:
6.154703e-05 vs 6.331829e-05
0.0007477905 vs 7.456714e-04

Where am I going wrong?

messages.body_plain:
Note that inla() has a 'quantile' argument.

You are using inla.tmarginal() with the identity function. That might distort the marginal slightly. Try inla.qmarginal(c(0.025,0.975), inla1$marginals.fixed[[2]]))

messages.body_plain:
they are computed with different finite representation. the one in the
inla output should be more correct.

if you want 90% intervals, you can add

     inla(
         formula,
         family = "gaussian",
         contrasts = NULL,
         data,
         quantiles=c(0.025, 0.5, 0.975),
         E = NULL,

to the quantiles argument, like

quantiles = c(0.025, 0.05, 0.5, 0.90, 0.975)

messages.body_plain:
Just a short follow up, in case this rings a bell for anyone.

I am still unable to fully make sense of the output of my hyperparameters. But in another model I was able to resolve the issue with the range, but at the cost of having another hyperparameter with way of the normal range :

Meanwhile I've done the model selection for another response (inverse Simpson index) from the same data-set (same mesh, same prior median range, but slightly different sd for the SPDE and not a poisson, but gaussian model).
There, the best fitting model (f1 below) has the spatio-temporal term, too (like the best fitting model for species richness). But, judging by DIC & WAIC the best model for inverse Simpson included a temporal random effect and a temporal autocorrelated effect. In f1, the issue with the huge range that I had with the model for species richness is gone - I have a range which makes somewhat sense. However, now the precision of the for my temporal random term is extremely high.

Out of curiosity, I also made a model including the effects for the best model for species richness (f2 below) so this model contains only the effects of the model in the previous emails (spatio-temporal effect and iid effect) - there the huge range for the spatial random effect is suddenly back to what it was in the other model.

I find this odd, as I would not expect that adding another separable temporal term should be able to reduce the range of the spatial correlation so much (or not having it in the model sould increase it by an order of magnitude), which makes me suspect that there may be something fundamentally wrong with my setup? Any suggestions on how to proceed to diagnose, what's going on here? I'm really not making any progress here with fixing this alone unfortunately.

Best,
Vincent

messages.subject: latent differences between levels of categorical predictor
messages.subject_clean: latent differences between levels of categorical predictor
messages.body_plain:
I have a model of counts that is potentially simple but has nuances that might benefit from additional latent variable structures.

Assume we have an after-school program in which 100 students compete.  For simplicity, we will say that they succeed or fail in each matchup, and compete in a number of matchups over the course of the program.  The matchups are not head-to-head.  The students are sorted by ability, into classes 1 through 5, with 1 being the lowest and 5 the highest. Students compete only against others in their class, and they participate at different frequencies.  This results in varying numbers of binomial trials per student per class. Many, but not all students participate at multiple levels over the course of the program.

What we want to know at any given time is how each student would be expected to perform, on average, if they were forced to compete at the highest level, which is the ultimate goal of the program.

I put together the following simulated dataset and basic model:

### load packages

library(tidyverse)

library(INLA)

### reproducibility

set.seed(4567)

### simulated predictors

# trials and success rates by level

df <- tibble(trials = round(runif(2e3, min=1, max=250)),

             success = rbinom(2e3, size=trials, prob=.4),

             class=1) %>%

  dplyr::bind_rows(tibble(trials = round(runif(2e3, min=1, max=250)),

                          success = rbinom(2e3, size=trials, prob=.5),

                          class=2)) %>%

  dplyr::bind_rows(tibble(trials = round(runif(2e3, min=1, max=250)),

                          success = rbinom(2e3, size=trials, prob=.6),

                          class=3)) %>%

  dplyr::bind_rows(tibble(trials = round(runif(2e3, min=1, max=250)),

                          success = rbinom(2e3, size=trials, prob=.7),

                          class=4)) %>%

  dplyr::bind_rows(tibble(trials = round(runif(2e3, min=1, max=250)),

                          success = rbinom(2e3, size=trials, prob=.8),

                          class=5))

# simulated students with varying abilities

student.dat <- tibble(

  ID = seq.int <http://seq.int>(1:1e2),

  ability = sample(c(-.5, -.25, 0, .25, .5), size=1e2, replace=TRUE))

# create the data frame to be modeled

df <- df %>%

  dplyr::bind_cols(dplyr::sample_n(student.dat, size=1e4, replace=TRUE))

# data frame to predict for each student at the highest level

df.preds <- expand.grid(success = NA,

                        class = 1,

                        ID = seq.int <http://seq.int>(1:100),

                        trials = 1)

### the basic model

samp.mod <- inla(success ~

                   offset(ability) + # to differentiate simulated students

                   class +

                   f(ID, model="iid"),

                 data=df %>%

                   dplyr::bind_rows(df.preds) %>%

                   dplyr::mutate(class = as.factor(class)),

                 family="binomial", Ntrials=trials,

                 control.predictor = list(link=1)

                 # verbose=TRUE

)

### extract and view predictions for success

df.preds$pred_success <- round(samp.mod$summary.fitted.values[10001:10100,]$mean,3)

df.preds$pred_success_sd <- round(samp.mod$summary.fitted.values[10001:10100,]$sd,3)

df.preds$success <- NULL

head(df.preds, n=20)

Although this model feels like a good start, there are important aspects of the relationships between levels that this model might not capture, but which I suspect INLA has the additional tools to track.

The first challenge is that, while the simple model captures the *mean* performance at each level of “class,” it doesn’t necessarily reflect the *differences* in difficulties between levels.  For that, we probably want to also track of the performance of students who switch classes.  But limiting the model to those students is undesirable because the students who don’t switch classes also give us useful information about the students not good enough to move up, and because we want to make the best possible predictions on all 100 students, whether they moved up previously or not.

It feels like this could employ a “lag” system that indexes differences between students who switch classes.  If so, perhaps this could be an autogression type of specification, maybe using the replicate function, but it could use discrete performances at different classes rather than different time measurements.  But not everyone switches classes, so I am not sure if this is really the best option, and again it is trying to use a “class” series rather than a “time” series.

The second challenge is that it is possible students could  “master” a class of difficulty and over-perform in a way that is not translatable to a higher level. In other words, they may not end up being properly “shrunk” toward the probable ability mean by the simple model because they spend a lot of trials running up the score to an unusual extent at a lower level.  So, for example, the true penalty of moving up one level might only be a few points of success on average, but somebody with a high number of trials and a level-specific amount of success could plummet far more than average when moved up. That’s the sort of thing we want to be aware of before putting a kid in a position to fail.

For this second problem, the challenge seems to be also modeling the maximum number of “trials” at each level that are actually useful in predicting success at a different level, although perhaps there is another way to approach it.  I am honestly not sure if there is a simple structure that could model this (perhaps a binned random walk on trials replicated to levels, with trials being an additional predictor in the model?), but am open to ideas.

I’d appreciate any suggestions the list has, especially if they allow this problem to be addressed within a single likelihood.

Jonathan

messages.subject: prior for phi in model bym2
messages.subject_clean: prior for phi in model bym2
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I'm trying to visualise the prior distribution for the mixing parameter phi in the 'bym2' model.

I thought that the (hidden) function INLA:::inla.pc.bym.phi() would give what I wanted, but I discovered that it can yield negative values. Is it returning the log of the prior density, perhaps ? So that exp(prior(x)) gives the actual density value of the prior? It looks that it integrates to 1 as expected if that was the case (see code below).

Can you confirm, please ?

Thanks!

ƒacu.-

phi = 1/(1+exp(-seq(-10, 10, len=1000)))
graph  <- system.file("demodata/germany.graph", package="INLA")
prior = INLA:::inla.pc.bym.phi(graph = graph, alpha = 2/3)

## Takes negative values!
plot(phi, prior(phi), type="l",  lwd=2, main = graph)
prior(.8) # < 0

## Is this a log-prior ?
plot(phi, exp(prior(phi)), type="l",  lwd=2, main = graph)

## At the very least, it integrates to 1
integrate(function(x) exp(prior(x)), 1e-8, 1-1e-08)

messages.body_plain:
I really appreciate all users helping me to use INLA models for my research.

I made a random slope model for spatio-temporal interaction, e.g.,

inla_fit <- inla(formula = y ~ x1 + x2 + ... + f(GEOID, xp, group=year, graph = graph, control.group=list(model = 'ar1'), constr=TRUE), data = data, ...)

Here I want to extract the slope of xp indicating the spatio-temporal interaction in terms of GEOID (limited by the graph object) and year.
The model result inla_fit should have summary.random, but inla_fit$summary.random$GEOID has the double number of rows with duplicate GEOIDs in the ID field, for example,

> inla_fit$summary.random$GEOID
> ID  mean ...
   1  ...
  ... ...
  10  ...
   1  ...
  ... ...
  10  ...

Which rows can be considered as slopes (other than iid component)? I read the Blangiardo and Cameletti (2015) text for several times, but the extraction of slope component from summary.random is not clearly stated, as far as I read.

Thank you very much in advance.

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] crashes with gpoisson likelihood
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] crashes with gpoisson likelihood
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

the error says that you run out of memory for some reason. The
question is why. Normally this is because the latent model is to
large, for which you can check by running the same model with
'poisson' instead of 'gpoisson'. I check the code for 'gpoisson' and
there is no memory leaks there (not any alloc at all), so its not for
that reason. (or running the model on a subset of the data)

Reading the documentation, there are quite some warnings about the
parameter 'p', maybe there should be a well defined prior like the PC-
prior constructed for it, but otherwise, please check if these 'notes'
might appear in your problem.

Otherwise, reducing the number of threads (num.threads=...)  and
setting  control.inla=list(strategy='adaptive',int.strategy='eb')
might help

Let me know.

H

> Dear all,
>
> I'm trying to visualise the prior distribution for the mixing
> parameter phi in the 'bym2' model.
>
> I thought that the (hidden) function INLA:::inla.pc.bym.phi() would
> give what I wanted, but I discovered that it can yield negative
> values. Is it returning the log of the prior density, perhaps ? So
> that exp(prior(x)) gives the actual density value of the prior? It
> looks that it integrates to 1 as expected if that was the case (see
> code below).
>
> Can you confirm, please ?
>
> Thanks!
>
> ƒacu.-
>
>
> phi = 1/(1+exp(-seq(-10, 10, len=1000)))
> graph  <- system.file("demodata/germany.graph", package="INLA")
> prior = INLA:::inla.pc.bym.phi(graph = graph, alpha = 2/3)
>
> ## Takes negative values!
> plot(phi, prior(phi), type="l",  lwd=2, main = graph)
> prior(.8) # < 0
>
> ## Is this a log-prior ?
> plot(phi, exp(prior(phi)), type="l",  lwd=2, main = graph)
>
> ## At the very least, it integrates to 1
> integrate(function(x) exp(prior(x)), 1e-8, 1-1e-08)
>

messages.body_plain:
yes.

can you register for the pardiso library; do

	inla.pardiso()

and follow the instructions.

reduce the number of threads ?

messages.subject: Multivariate Joint Hurdle Model
messages.subject_clean: Multivariate Joint Hurdle Model
messages.body_plain:
I want to make bivariate hurdle model with both zero model and count model outputs at the same time. There are three fixed efeects. Is anyone can help me to correct this code please?

coords <- as.matrix(Dataset[,c(8,9])

bnd = inla.nonconvex.hull(coords, convex = 0.09)

mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(boundary = bnd, loc = coords, max.edge=c(0.14, 0.07))

spde = inla.spde2.matern(mesh, constr = TRUE)

A <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh=mesh, loc=coords)

Year = Dataset$Year

Fixed1 = scale(Dataset$Fixed1)

Fixed2 = scale(Dataset$Fixed2)

s1 <- count1

s2 <- count2

z1 <- (s1>0) + 0

y1 <- ifelse(s1>0, s1, NA)

z2 <- (s2>0) + 0

y2 <- ifelse(s2>0, s2, NA)

n =n

n.y1 <- length(which(s1 > 0))

n.y2 <- length(which(s2 > 0))

n.z1 <- length(which(s1 == 0))

n.z2 <- length(which(s2 == 0))

n.y <- length(which(s1 > 0 | s2 > 0))

n.z <- length(which(s1 == 0 & s2 == 0))

Fixed1.z <- c(Fixed1[which(s1 == 0 & s2 == 0)], rep(NA,n.y))

Fixed1.y <- c(rep(NA, n.z), Fixed1[which(s1 > 0 | s2 > 0)])

Fixed2.z <- c(Fixed2[which(s1 == 0 & s2 == 0)], rep(NA,n.y))

Fixed2.y <- c(rep(NA, n.z), Fixed2[which(s1 > 0 | s2 > 0)])

stk.z1 <- inla.stack(tag='BFD.z', data=list(y=cbind(z1,NA,NA,NA)),

                     A=list(A, 1, 1, 1),

                     effects=list(s=1:mesh$n, mu.z1=rep(1, length(z1)),

                     list(Fixed1.z=Fixed1.z, Fixed2.z=Fixed2.z), Year=c(rep(NA, n.z),Year[which(s1 >0 | s2 > 0)])))

stk.y1 <- inla.stack(tag="BFD.y", data=list(y=cbind(NA,y1,NA,NA)),

                     A=list(A, 1, 1),

                     effects=list(s=1:mesh$n, list(mu.y1=rep(1, length(y1))),

                     list(Fixed1.z=Fixed1.z, Fixed2.z=Fixed2.z), Year=c(rep(NA, n.z),Year[which(s1 >0 | s2 > 0)]))))

stk.z2 <- inla.stack(tag='BWS.z', data=list(y=cbind(NA,NA,z2,NA)),

                     A=list(A, 1, 1),

                     effects=list(s=1:mesh$n, list(mu.z2=rep(1, length(z2))),

                     list(Fixed1.z=Fixed1.z, Fixed2.z=Fixed2.z), Year=c(rep(NA, n.z),Year[which(s1 >0 | s2 > 0)]))))

stk.y2 <- inla.stack(tag="BWS.y", data=list(y=cbind(NA,NA,NA,y2)),

                     A=list(A, 1, 1),

                     effects=list(s=1:mesh$n, list(mu.y2=rep(1, length(y2))),

                     list(Fixed1.z=Fixed1.z, Fixed2.z=Fixed2.z), Year=c(rep(NA, n.z),Year[which(s1 >0 | s2 > 0)]))))

stack.zy = inla.stack(stk.z1, stk.y1, stk.z2, stk.y2)

formula.zy <- y ~ 0 + mu.y1 + mu.z1 + mu.y2 + mu.z2 + temp.z + rainfall.z + Rpop.z + Vpop.z + temp.y + rainfall.y + Rpop.y + Vpop.y + f(s, model = spde) + f(Year, model = "ar1")

result <- inla(formula.zy,

               family = rep(c("binomial","zeroinflatednbinomial0"),2),

               data = inla.stack.data(stack.zy),

               control.predictor=list(A=inla.stack.A(stack.zy), compute=TRUE),

               control.compute = list(dic=TRUE,cpo=TRUE, po=TRUE))

summary(result)

Thank you in advance.
